issues.legal_issue: A court cannot treat property as joint-family property merely because a Hindu joint family exists when the property’s joint-family character was not pleaded or supported by an issue and evidence.
material_facts: The pleadings did not allege that the properties gifted by the husband to his wife were joint-family properties.
No issue was framed on whether the properties were joint-family properties, and the evidence did not establish that character.
The lower courts nevertheless treated the properties as joint-family properties.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the properties were joint-family properties was unwarranted. The existence of a Hindu joint family may be presumed, but the existence of joint-family property cannot be presumed from that fact alone.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the principles that a finding must be supported by the pleadings, issues, and evidence, and that a presumption of a Hindu joint family does not itself create a presumption that the family owns joint-family property. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for these principles.

rule.if: property_title_appeal and joint_family_character_not_pleaded and no_joint_family_issue and no_evidence_of_joint_family_character

predicates.property_title_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a dispute over title to property.
predicates.joint_family_character_not_pleaded: The party asserting that the disputed property is joint-family property did not plead that the property had that character.
predicates.no_joint_family_issue: The court did not frame an issue on whether the disputed property was joint-family property.
predicates.no_evidence_of_joint_family_character: The evidence did not establish that the disputed property was joint-family property.

issues.definition: When a property-title appeal concerns property whose joint-family character was neither pleaded, put in issue, nor established by evidence, the finding that it is joint-family property is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: A deed granting property to a wife in absolute terms transfers full ownership to her, and a recital explaining the circumstances of the gift does not make the gift a trust or a transfer to the son.
material_facts: The husband’s deed stated that he gifted the scheduled property to his wife and that she could enjoy it with absolute rights.
The deed referred to the wife’s minor son and her wish to be provided for, but the court found that this recital explained the circumstances prompting the gift.
The deed did not express an intention to create a trust for the son or convey the husband’s share to him.
issues.conclusion: The deed was a valid absolute gift to the wife, who acquired full title to the properties.
issues.legal_principle: The court construed the deed according to its clear and unequivocal terms: an absolute grant to the wife was not converted into a trust or a conveyance to the son merely by mentioning him in the recital. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this construction.

predicates.property_gift_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over title to property transferred by a gift deed.
predicates.deed_grants_absolute_ownership: The gift deed expressly grants the recipient absolute ownership of the property.
predicates.son_is_mentioned_only_as_gift_context: The deed mentions the donor’s son as part of the circumstances explaining the gift, without expressing an intention to benefit him or create a trust for him.

issues.definition: When a gift deed in a property-title dispute expressly grants absolute ownership to the wife and mentions the son only to explain the gift, the wife acquires full title.

issues.legal_issue: A recipient who obtains full ownership by gift may transfer the property, and a purchaser from that recipient acquires title to the property validly sold.
material_facts: The wife acquired full title under her husband’s gift deed.
She later gifted the properties to her granddaughter, who was also her daughter-in-law, with full rights.
That recipient exchanged part of the gifted property with her husband and retained the remaining properties.
She sold the retained properties to the appellant, who brought the title-and-possession suit.
The husband’s competing sale to the defendant had occurred before the appellant’s purchase, but the husband did not own the properties transferred through the valid gift chain.
issues.conclusion: The recipient of the later gift became full owner and could dispose of the property. Her sale to the appellant validly transferred title, and the appellant acquired proper title to the properties sold to him.
issues.legal_principle: A person who owns property absolutely may deal with and dispose of it; a valid transfer by that owner passes title to the transferee. The court applied this principle to the successive gifts, exchange, and sale. It did not need to decide whether the husband or a person claiming through him was estopped from challenging the wife’s title. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: property_title_appeal and transferor_has_full_title and later_gift_conveys_full_rights and recipient_retains_property_after_exchange and recipient_sells_retained_property

predicates.property_title_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a dispute over title to property.
predicates.transferor_has_full_title: The person who makes the later gift owns the property in full.
predicates.later_gift_conveys_full_rights: The later gift transfers full ownership rights to its recipient.
predicates.recipient_retains_property_after_exchang: The recipient of the later gift exchanges part of the property and retains the rest.
predicates.recipient_sells_retained_property: The recipient sells the retained property to the purchaser.

issues.definition: When a fully entitled owner gifts property with full rights, the recipient retains some of it after an exchange, and then sells that retained property, the purchaser acquires valid title.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding an appeal cannot disregard unchallenged findings made after remand on whether an exchange was acted upon and who possessed the property.
material_facts: The High Court remanded the matter for findings on whether the exchange was nominal and whether the plaintiff was in possession on the suit date.
After considering the evidence, the lower appellate court found that the exchange had been acted upon and that the plaintiff was in possession.
Those findings were not challenged, but the High Court dismissed the appeal without giving them effect.
issues.conclusion: The findings after remand were unchallenged and final, and the High Court erred in ignoring them.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated the unchallenged findings made pursuant to the remand as final in the appeal and held that they could not be ignored. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.civil_appeal_after_remand: The proceeding is a civil appeal following a remand for further findings.
predicates.lower_court_makes_findings_within_remand: The lower court makes findings on the matters referred to it by the remand.
predicates.findings_are_not_challenged: The parties do not challenge those findings in the appeal.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal after remand, findings made within the remand’s scope and left unchallenged are final.
